newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan, Iraq seek to improve ties in coming phase.
newsitem.headline: Jordan, Iraq seek to improve ties in coming phase.

text.p: Jordan and Iraq said on Saturday they hoped to bolster ties under the new Jordanian government, after its predecessor brought bilateral ties to their lowest point in years.

"We want to improve ties with Jordan and lead it in its brotherly path that attains the joint interests of the two countries, as was the case for many years," Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz told reporters after talks with newly appointed Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali.

The king last Wednesday brought back Majali, who signed the peace treaty with Israel when he was prime minister in 1994, after abruptly sacking outgoing Prime Minster Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, a move that political observers linked to differences over Israel.

Jordan had good relations with Iraq during Majali's period in office in 1993-1995. King Hussein, a close ally of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein during the 1990 Gulf crisis, subsequently turned against the Iraqi ruler and Kabariti was seen as spearheading that move.
"I have extended my congratulations to Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, who is friend and old colleague whom we have worked with for a long time," Aziz said.
Kabariti, taking his cue from the king, steered Jordan away from close political and economic ties with Baghdad in a shift towards former Arab Gulf allies and better ties with the West.

Jordanian officials hope the new Majali government will improve the political atmosphere with Baghdad, which did not hide its discomfort from Kabariti for voicing strong anti-Baghdad statements at the height of tense ties.

Asked about tension in Iraqi-Jordanian ties during Kabariti's 13-month premiership, Aziz said: "I don't think there was tension but maybe an artificially provoked tension.. there is a difference between tension and artificially creating it."
Referring to Kabariti, Aziz said it was only "natural" that ties would expand under a new Jordanian government.

Aziz, heading to Baghdad after a European tour, told reporters his country welcomed any Arab effort, including Jordanian, to end a strict U.N. trade embargo enforced against Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Majali was quoted by the state news agency as saying Jordan "hoped that the suffering of the Iraqi people would come to an end to allow Iraq to resume its role in the region."

Since Iraq signed a deal with the United Nations allowing it to export oil worth $2 billion every six months to buy food and medicines, Jordan's business community has been campaigning for better ties with Baghdad to help them secure contracts.

Officials said Jordan, which comes after France in securing deals under the oil-for-food deal with over $120 million of orders, was notified on Saturday by the U.N. sanctions committee it had finally approved $26 million long-delayed signed contracts by firms selling detergents and soaps to Baghdad.

Jordan's Minister of Trade Hani al-Mulqi told an Iraqi delegation led by Adnan Qudsi, chairman of the private sector Union of Iraqi Industries, that Amman seeks to boost private sector commerce with Iraq in 1997, beyond a limiting $220 annual trade protocol which barters goods for Iraqi oil.
